- When sentiment is strongly negative (e.g., < -0.5) over recent days, model tends to overcorrect downward — adjust forecast upward slightly to avoid excessive sell-off bias.  
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., >+1.5% from prior day), model often overshoots and fails to correct — reduce forecast peak by 5–10% and add a slight downward slope to avoid overreaction.  
- If sentiment is neutral or mildly positive (e.g., 0 to +0.3), model tends to underestimate true price — increase forecast by 2–5% to capture mean reversion toward higher levels.  
- Model consistently underestimates true price in early horizon (e.g., 1–3 days ahead) — apply a small upward bias (e.g., +0.5–1.5%) to compensate for lag.  
- When sentiment is volatile or erratic (e.g., alternating +/–0.3+), model overfits short-term noise — smooth forecast by averaging last 3–5 days’ values to reduce false peaks.  
- If true price is consistently higher than forecast (e.g., >+0.8% over 3–5 days), model exhibits mean reversion bias — increase forecast by 1–3% to align with recent upward momentum.
